public_rationale: The condition held: by October 2025, 21% of the Shorts shown to a new YouTube account were AI-generated (e5). Studies of ordinary viewers then found that people mostly cannot tell modern AI video from real footage. In Runway's study of 1,043 people, overall accuracy was 57.1%, and over 90% could not reliably tell the difference (e1). An academic preprint found 52.6% accuracy on modern fakes (e2). A peer-reviewed study of 1,276 people found near-chance detection (e3). Counterevidence: a 40-person eye-tracking study found 66.4% accuracy (e4), so viewers are not at pure chance. Read plainly, "no idea" means not being able to reliably tell real from fake, and most evidence supports that. Taken literally, it overstates the case a little.
limitations: "No idea" is hyperbole. Measured accuracy runs from about 52% to 66%, not exactly chance.
The key large study (e1) was published by a company that sells video generation.
Lab conditions differ from real platform viewing.
Some studies use narrow content types (for example, public-speaking videos in e2).

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Once photorealistic AI fake videos spread, the average user will be unable to tell which videos are legitimate and which are fake.
conditions: once photorealistic AI fake videos proliferate

statement.document_title: Absolutely amazing ant video augurs intellectual mayhem

from_speaker: "will have no idea what is and is not legit"

our_interpretation: Condition: photorealistic AI-generated videos have become common on major video platforms such as YouTube.

Plain reading of "no idea": ordinary viewers cannot reliably tell real videos from current photorealistic AI videos. In studies, that means average accuracy near chance (roughly 50-60%) or most people unable to reach reliable accuracy. It does not require exactly 50%.
Evidence: controlled studies of ordinary or general-population viewers that use current-generation video models.
criteria.support_condition: After AI videos have become common on platforms, studies of ordinary viewers find average real-vs-AI video accuracy near chance, or find that most participants cannot reliably tell the two apart.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Studies of ordinary viewers using current photorealistic AI videos find that average viewers reliably tell them apart from real footage (for example 75% accuracy or higher).

evidence.excerpt: Only 99 of 1,043 participants (9.5%) achieved statistically significant accuracy (≥15/20 correct, p < 0.05, binomial test). Overall detection accuracy was 57.1%, only slightly above chance.
evidence.explanation: In a random sample of 1,043 people, overall accuracy was 57.1% and over 90% could not reliably tell real video from AI video. This fits the plain reading of the claim. The publisher is a video-model vendor.

evidence.excerpt: accuracy on fake videos drops to 52.6% on DF26, barely above chance
evidence.explanation: An academic human study found that people spotted modern AI-generated speaking videos only at about chance level. Real videos were still judged correctly about 73% of the time.

evidence.excerpt: people struggled to distinguish between synthetic and authentic media, with the mean detection performance close to a chance level performance of 50%.
evidence.publisher: arXiv / Communications of the ACM (Cooke et al.)
evidence.explanation: A peer-reviewed study of 1,276 participants found near-chance detection across images, video and audio. It came early in the period and does not isolate the newest video models.

evidence.excerpt: The majority of participants (36 out of 40) performed better than the random guess baseline of 50%. The mean accuracy across participants was 66.4%.
evidence.locator: section Results, Judgment-dependent gaze behaviors, paragraph 2
evidence.explanation: In a small lab study, most participants did better than chance (mean 66.4%). This suggests that attentive viewers have some ability to spot AI videos.

evidence.excerpt: in total, 104 (21%) of the first 500 videos were AI-generated
evidence.locator: section On A New YouTube Feed, 33% of Videos are Brainrot
evidence.explanation: About a fifth of the Shorts served to a new YouTube account were AI-generated. This shows the condition (AI video spreading on platforms such as YouTube) had been met.

conclusive_event.meets_rule: After AI videos were common on platforms, a study of 1,043 participants found 57.1% overall accuracy, and over 90% could not reliably distinguish real from AI video. That is near chance for average viewers.
